claims.text: The conventionally cast eutectic high-entropy alloy has dual-phase lamellar colonies containing numerous internal boundaries.
Internal lamellar or colony boundaries are prone to microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
Adding approximately 0.5–1.0 at% boron during alloy processing will cause boron to segregate preferentially to colony boundaries during homogenization.
Homogenization at about 1200°C for 1 hour will provide adequate conditions for boron segregation.
Boron segregation will enhance interfacial cohesion along lamellar colony boundaries.
Boron addition may produce fine-scale boron-enriched features that resist boundary decohesion.
Trace boron is known to segregate to internal boundaries during homogenization.
Boron segregation reduces local stress concentrations at internal boundaries.
Reduced boundary energy and local stress concentrations suppress microcrack initiation.
A refined boron-modified interfacial structure contributes to precipitation strengthening.
Trace boron addition will increase yield strength relative to the unmodified alloy.
Trace boron addition will increase room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the unmodified alloy.
More cohesive boundaries will delay crack initiation and thereby enhance tensile ductility.
The unmodified alloy has high strength but limited tensile ductility because microcracks cause brittle failure.
The intervention is expected to apply to eutectic high-entropy alloys having a lamellar morphology.
Keeping boron below approximately 1.0 at% will avoid detrimental brittle boride formation.
Successful strengthening and ductilization require adequate boron segregation without adverse alteration of the overall microstructure.
